summary: Johann Gildemeister worked in Indology. He studied at Göttingen under Heinrich Ewald (~1832–1834) and at Bonn under Georg Freytag, Christian Lassen, and August Wilhelm von Schlegel (~1834–1838). He held professorships at Marburg (~1845–1859) and Bonn (~1859–1890).

Johann Gottfried Eichhorn worked in religious studies, history/archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at Göttingen under Christian Gottlob Heyne (1770–1774). He served as professor of Oriental languages at Jena (1775) and professor of philosophy at Göttingen (1788).

Johann Gottfried Ludwig Kosegarten specialized in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Greifswald (1808) and under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy (1812). He held posts at Greifswald (adjunct 1815, professor 1824–1850) and Jena (professor 1817–1824).

Johann Gottfried von Herder was a scholar of philosophy, linguistics, and religious studies. He studied theology at Königsberg (1761). His posts included teaching at Riga Cathedral School (1764–1769), general superintendent at Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach (1776), and director at Wilhelm-Ernst-Gymnasium Weimar (~1776–1803).

Johann Gustav Stickel worked in linguistics. He studied at the University of Jena (1823–1826) under Johann Gottfried Ludwig Kosegarten (~1824–1827) and under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy (~1828–1829). He later served as professor at Jena (1830–1836).
Johann II Bernoulli studied at the University of Basel (~1724–1729). He later held a post there from circa 1743 to 1790.

Johann III Bernoulli was active in Indology and history/archaeology. He studied at Neuchâtel and Basel (~1757–1758), studying under Daniel Bernoulli (~1757–1763). He held memberships at the Prussian (1764) and Russian (1776) Academies of Sciences.
Johann Jakob Engel was a philosopher who studied at the University of Rostock (~1758–1762) and the University of Leipzig (~1762–1765).

Johann Tobias Beck was a religious studies scholar who studied at the University of Tübingen (~1822–1826). He held posts at the University of Basel (~1836–1843) and the University of Tübingen (~1843–1878).

Johann Wilhelm Andreas Pfaff worked in Indology and other fields after studying at Tübingen (~1793–1797). He held posts at the University of Tartu (~1803–1809), University of Würzburg (~1815–1818), and University of Erlangen-Nuremberg (~1818–1835).

Johanna Engelberta van Lohuizen-de Leeuw worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. She studied at Leiden and Utrecht (doctoral degree under Jan Gonda, ~1946–1949). She held posts at Cambridge (1951–1959) and the University of Amsterdam (1958–1983).

Johanna Narten specialized in linguistics, Iranian/Central Asian studies, and Indology. She studied at Saarland under Ernst Zinn (1951) and at Erlangen-Nuremberg under Karl Hoffmann (PhD 1955–1961, Habilitation ~1961–1971), later serving as an assistant there (1973–1977).

Johannes Beltz works in Indology, religious studies, and Buddhist studies. He completed doctoral studies under Johannes Bronkhorst and Marie-Louise Reiniche at the University of Lausanne and the École Pratique des Hautes Études, finishing by 1999.

Johannes Bronkhorst works in Indology, Buddhist studies, and philosophy. He studied at Pune (PhD under S. D. Joshi, ~1976–1979) and Leiden (doctorate ~1979–1980). He held posts at the Kern Institute (~1980–1987) and Lausanne (1987–2011; ~1987–2025).

Johannes Gijsbertus de Casparis specialized in Indology and history/archaeology. He studied at Leiden University (~1934–1939) and later held posts at SOAS University of London (~1964–1981) and Leiden University (1978–1986).

Johannes Hertel was an Indologist who earned his doctorate at Leipzig (1892–1897). He taught at Lessing-Gymnasium Döbeln (~1898–1920) and held the chair of Indian philology at the University of Leipzig (1919–1937).

Johannes Klatt was an Indologist who studied under Albrecht Weber (1868–1872) and earned a doctorate at Halle-Wittenberg (~1869–1873). He worked at the Royal Library of Berlin as staff, assistant, custodian, and librarian between 1872 and 1889.

Johannes Nobel worked in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology. He studied at Greifswald and Berlin (PhD under Heinrich Lüders, 1908–1911). He held positions at Berlin (1921, 1927) and the chair of Indology at Marburg (1928–1955).

Johannes Rahder worked in Indology, Japanology, and Buddhist studies, earning a doctorate at Utrecht (~1920–1926). He held posts at Utrecht (professor, 1930–1931), Leiden (chair of Japanese, 1931–1946), and Yale (professor, 1947–1965).

Johannes Schmidt worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied at Bonn, Jena, and under August Schleicher, Albrecht Weber, F. W. Ritschl, and Otto Jahn. He held professorships at Bonn (1868), Graz (1873–1876), and Berlin (1876).
